consensus_summary: The blind consensus holds that a 'new name' symbolizes a new, God-given identity, character, and status conferred on the redeemed—marking transformation, covenant belonging, and eschatological vindication—grounded in Rev 2:17; 3:12; Isa 62:2; 65:15; and OT renaming narratives (Abram/Abraham, Jacob/Israel). Common sub-readings include divine ownership, intimate private communion (the name known only to its recipient), and corporate restoration of Zion.
book_summary: The book defines the new name as a newly conferred covenant identity under its giver—an identity that is known, received, and kept only by the one who bears it—citing Gen 32:28; Isa 62:2-5; 65:15; Rev 2:17. Its common-view note ('a new God-given identity and character bestowed on the overcomer') matches the consensus.
consensus_core_identification: A divinely bestowed new identity/status signifying transformation, covenant belonging, and vindication.
book_core_identification: A divinely conferred covenant identity, personally and privately possessed by its bearer.
boundary_disagreement: Minimal. The book folds the Rev 2:17 privacy motif ('which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it') into its definition, whereas the consensus treats private/intimate knowledge as a common complementary sub-reading rather than a definitional feature. This is emphasis, not exclusion of cases: both readings cover the same renaming texts (Jacob/Israel, Zion, the overcomer).
material_contradiction: None. The book's 'covenant identity under its giver' is exactly the consensus's God-conferred identity and covenant belonging, and the exclusivity clause is drawn directly from Rev 2:17, which the consensus already incorporates.
rationale: Reduced to minimum cores, both readings identify the new name as a newly bestowed identity conferred by God within covenant relationship. The book's added clause about the name being known and kept only by its bearer restates a feature the consensus explicitly lists (Rev 2:17 intimacy reading, prominence 'common') rather than reclassifying or excluding any cases. The book's own common-view note is nearly verbatim the consensus primary meaning, and its cited texts overlap the consensus basis. Differences are wording and emphasis, not extension or referent.
strongest_objection: One could argue REFINED: by making exclusive private knowledge definitional ('known...only by the one who bears it'), the book universalizes a Rev 2:17-specific feature to cases like Jacob/Israel and Zion, whose new names were publicly known (Isa 62:2 says kings and nations will see and use the name), which could be a material boundary shift rather than mere emphasis.
